Materials and methods
Materials
Analytical  grade  reagents  and  chemicals  were  used  in  this  study.  Chemical  magnesium  nitrate  (99%  purity), 
Zinc acetate dehydrate (98% purity), and NaOH (98%) were purchased from Spectrum Reagents and Chemicals 
Pvt.  Ltd.  (India),  respectively.  Pure  Chia  seeds  and  Rosemary  leaves  were  purchased  from  a  branded  online 
store, Neutra Veda. Fresh Neem leaves were collected from the campus of Madan Mohan Malaviya University 
of Technology. The Rosemary leaves were about 100% pure as per supplier’s data. Solutions were prepared using 
distilled water. Their detailed discussion of the methodology is as follows.

Synthesis of MgO and ZnO NPs
The preparation of NPs using plant extracts has several advantages. This reduced the use of reactive chemicals. 
Chia  (Salvia  hispanica  L.)  belongs  to  the  Lamiaceae  family  of  the  plant  kingdom,  with  characteristics  of  an 
annual herbaceous plant. Chia is well known as a source of oil, protein, dietary fibre, minerals, and polyphenolic 
compounds with medicinal value, which is consumed as oilseed, flour, whole seeds, and mucilage. The oil content 
of the Chia seeds with enhanced polyunsaturated omega-3-linolenic acid is the major cause for the increasing 
interest  of  the  consumers.  In  addition,  Chia  seeds  are  also  known  for  their  richness  in  natural  antioxidants 
such  as  tocopherols,  phytosterols,  carotenoids,  and  phenolic  compounds,  including  chlorogenic  acid,  caffeic 
acid,  myricetin,  quercetin,  and  kaempferol,  which  lead  to  benefits  on  human  health3.  The  presence  of  these 
phytochemicals make them biocompatible and useful for in vitro applications because our body does not react 
against their presence in form of traces left during synthesis if any. After washing Chia seeds multiple times 
with  distilled  water  and  allowing  them  to  dry,  we  took  3  g  of  Chiaseeds  (Salvia  hispanica  L.)  in  100  mL  of 
distilled water (DW). The mixture was then stirred at 60 °C for 2 h. The aqueous extract was then filtered Fig. 2. 
Before synthesizing MgO-NPs, solution A (0.3 M Mg (NO3)2.6H2O) (100 mL) was prepared. Solution A was 
continuously stirred, and 10 mL of aqueous Salvia hispanica L. (Chia) extract was gradually added drop wise. 
The  resulting  mixture  was  stirred  for  18  and  1/2  hours  at  70  °C  because  temperature  offers  the  best  balance 
between  the  reaction  kinetics  and  precursor  stability.  70  °C  was  chosen  as  the  stirring  temperature  during 
MgO synthesis. In addition to facilitate homogeneous nucleation and the development of MgO particles, 70 °C 
improves  reactant  solubility  and  diffusion,  reducing  fast  component  evaporation  or  degradation.  It  has  been 
demonstrated that well-dispersed and uniform nanoparticles can be produced under these conditions40. Yellow 
residue in the beaker was filtered and calcined at 300 °C for 4 h, yielding the final white MgO nanopowder. The 
preparation of MgO NPs by the sol gel method is illustrated in Fig. 3.

chose the leaves of Dahlia Pinnata as they contain bioactive organic molecules and phytochemicals that may 
reduce the metal ions and stabilize the colloidal particles in the reacting solution41,42 Dahlia leaves were washed 
two or three times with distilled water. After letting the leaves dry for three hours at room temperature, they 
were mixed with 100 mL of deionised water to make a paste. The paste was spun at 800 rpm. Room temperature, 
or approximately 30 °C, was used to create the yellow-colored extract. The extract was filtered using a Whatman 
filter paper. Eventually, the color of the extract turned reddish brown.

Coating of nanoparticles on microtiter plates
Figure 8 (a) shows the coating scheme of 2,5-Dimercapto-1,3,4-thiadiazole on polystyrene microtiter plates. We 
mixed 100 mg of 2,5-Dimercapto-1,3,4-thiadiazole in 100 mL methanol and stirred for 20 min at 400 rpm. Then, 
we dropped the solution into the wells of microtiter plates and allowed the solvent to evaporate by maintaining 
a temperature of 60 °C in an oven for 24 h. We coated the functionalized plate with 2, 4, 6, 8, 12, and 16 mg of 
MgO and ZnO nanoparticles by dissolving them in 25 mL of distilled water. The solutions of ZnO and MgO 
NPs prepared in distilled water were evaporated by keeping the microtiter plate at 60 °C in an oven for 24 h. 
The concentrations C1, C2, C3, C4, and C5 were 2, 4, 6, 8, and 16 mg per 25 mL DW, respectively. The heating 
process not only allows the use of 2,5-Dimercapto-1,3,4-thiadiazole on the microtiter plate, but CDs and metal 
oxide nanoparticles also have ample opportunities to bind with the = S group present in 2,5-Dimercapto-1,3,4-
thiadiazole.

Biofilm production by crystal Violet biofilm assay
The 96-well microtiter plate made of polystyrene was used to detect biofilms. All the plates were kept at 60 °C for 
4 h before being used for the We first sterilized the 96-well microtiter plate and placed it in an oven at 60 °C for 
4 h and then used it for the biofilm growth process. Three isolates of Candida albicans recovered from clinical 
samples  were  used  after  approval  from  the  Institute’s  Human  Ethical  Clearance  Committee.  To  determine 
the impact on biofilm production, a crystal violet assay was conducted on microtiter plates with and without 
nanoparticles. The Crystal violet assay was performed as described previously by Marack et al.45. Briefly, fresh 
Candida albicans was inoculated in a tube containing two millilitres of brain heart infusion broth (BHIB), and 
the tubes were incubated at 37 °C. After overnight incubation, the broth cultures were diluted 1:20 using fresh 
BHIB. Microtiter plates were filled with 200 µl of diluted BHIB and incubated at 37 °C for 24 h. The microtiter 
plates were then emptied, washed thrice with distilled water, and inverted. Next, 200 µl of 1% crystal violet was 
added to each well and incubated for 15 min. Excess crystal violet was further removed after three washes with 
distilled water, and the dye was eluted by adding 200 µl of an 80:20 w/v ethanol: acetone mixture in each well 
and was read at 450 nm using an ELISA reader, and Optical Density (D) was recorded for each well. The optical 
density is defined as the log of the ratio of the intensities of the incident and transmitted light.

D = log10 (incident light / transmitted light)

Sterile  BHIB  without  microorganisms  was  used  as  a  negative  control.  The  cut-off  value  was  determined  by 
arithmetically averaging the OD of the wells containing sterile BHIB and adding a standard deviation of + 2. 
Samples with an OD higher than the cut-off value were considered positive, whereas those with a lower optical 
density than the cut-off were deemed to be negative45.

the tubes were incubated at 37 °C. After overnight incubation, the broth cultures were diluted 1:20 using fresh

distilled water, and the dye was eluted by adding 200 µl of an 80:20 w/v ethanol: acetone mixture in each well 
and was read at 450 nm using an ELISA reader, and Optical Density (D) was recorded for each well. The optical

density than the cut-off were deemed to be negative45.

plates were then emptied, washed thrice with distilled water, and inverted. Next, 200 µl of 1% crystal violet was 
added to each well and incubated for 15 min. Excess crystal violet was further removed after three washes with 
distilled water, and the dye was eluted by adding 200 µl of an 80:20 w/v ethanol: acetone mixture in each well 
and was read at 450 nm using an ELISA reader, and Optical Density (D) was recorded for each well. The optical 
density is defined as the log of the ratio of the intensities of the incident and transmitted light.

We’ve already explored how nanoparticles and carbon dots can suppress fungal growth, but there’s more to the 
story. These remarkable nanomaterials unleash a series of additional mechanisms that amplify their antifungal 
power, further tipping the scales in favor of inhibition. Here’s how they intensify their impact. Zeta potential 
affects the stability, surface charge, and interaction of nanoparticles with bacterial cell membranes, all of which 
are  crucial  to  their  antibacterial  efficacy.  Nanoparticles  with  high  positive  or  negative  zeta  potential  values 
typically exhibit superior colloidal stability to avoid aggregation and guarantee a wider surface area for contact 
with microbial cells. Oppositely charged pathogens adhere to the surface of nanoparticles, which prevents their 
growth and kill them by causing membrane breakdown, intracellular content leakage, ultimately leading to the 
cell death. Higher zeta potentials of nanoparticles prevent their agglomeration due to electrostatic repulsion, 
which in turn offers more surface area exposed to the fungal and bacterial pathogens and may enhance NPs 
efficacy if the pathogens are oppositely charged. Thus, the nanoparticle efficacy against pathogens also depends 
on the choice of the selection of their pair (i.e. all NPs will not show good inhibition properties against any 
pathogen). On the other hand, nanoparticles can combine together if their absolute zeta potential is low ( < ± 20 
mV), which would decrease their surface area and antibacterial activity. To improve the anti-microbial properties 
of nanoparticles, particularly in biomedical and environmental applications, it is imperative to optimize their 
zeta potential apart of wisely choosing them53.

open  the  doors  for  new  applications  at  very  low  cost  in  coming  future.  The  work  further  extends  the  idea 
published  in  recent  publication  in  scientific  reports57  which  suggests  for  the  unique  reorganization  of  NPs 
and QDs owing to the blending of weak dispersion force with that arsing due to NP interactions; a process in 
which plasmons can play a vital role. A nanodots array can agitate electrons in micro-organisms and may check 
their growth. That requires more work to confirm, since the process is least understood. Both qualitative and 
quantitative  confirmation  of  the  creation  of  nanoparticles  was  obtained  through  characterization  techniques 
and analysis. We successfully used green method to synthesize MgO and ZnO NPs and C-nanodots. With a 
particular emphasis on the inhibition of Candida albicans, this work elucidated the inhibitory characteristics of 
nanoparticle-coated functionalized microtiterplate surfaces, which can be used for further investigations. The 
same procedure can be adopted for other pair of pathogens and coating of NPs. This work could be helpful for 
scientists and researchers working in interdisciplinary areas to further exploit the methodology proposed in this 
work. In our case studies, we observe the cumulative influence of these factors, because the presence of the DMcT 
also serves as linking molecule for nanoparticles bringing them closer to form aggregated nano-microstructures. 
The emergence of sharp tip nano-micro-needles and saw like structures appear to show inhibition properties 
because  of  three  reasons:  (1)  high  surface  to  volume  ratio  and  higher  density  of  nanoparticles,  (2)  sharp  tip 
needle-shaped  and  blade-  like  nano-microstructures  composed  of  nanoparticles  and  (3)  interplaying  role  of 
zeta potential and interfacial interactions at nano and micro scales. The antifungal properties of metal oxide 
nanoparticles and carbon dots are currently understudied, indicating a need for more research in this area76. The 
formation of wavy nano-micro-structures with sharp edges as that of blades or even better, can pin down the 
fungi leading to the significant inhibition. The sharpest blades ever designed have dimensions as low as 3 nm. 
The metal blades with edge dimensions of with few tens of microns have been designed and are in use77. Candida 
albican fungi have sizes from 5 to 8 µ, typical bacteria have sizes 0.5 -5.0 µ and may have exceptional sizes up to 
2.0 cm, and viruses have sizes 5 nm to 300 nm. The atomistic sharp tip needle-shaped nanoparticles and nano-
sized saw-like structures with edges of a few tens of nanometres as presented in this paper may indeed contribute 
to enhance the anti-microbial properties and can be exploited for tailoring anti-fungal, anti-bacterial and ant-
vial properties on surfaces. The work is useful for diagnostic, therapeutic as well as for preventive healthcare 
services. The crystal violet bio-assay technique has already been in use for many decades for diagnostic purposes. 
Coating of anti-microbial agents on microtiter plates can help to estimate and quantify their doses appropriate 
enough to use as drugs for fighting against illness caused due to microbial diseases. Understanding such surface 
efficacy against pathogens may help to devise health care devices used in preventive health care units, which can 
prevent their growth and check at very early stages. Further finely tuned quantitative and critical study for many 
other cases may open the Pandora box.
